about: ROM hash -> patches. by_crc32 is keyed by the CRC32 of the ROM a patch needs (patches) or produces (produced_by). by_md5 / by_sha1 / by_sha256 map those hashes to the CRC32 key.

**Goraku Ou Tango!** (語楽王TANGO!) is Mebius's 1999 word puzzle for the original (monochrome) WonderSwan, published by Bandai and released only in Japan. Each puzzle gives you a category (home appliances, Japanese castles, rainbow colours...) and a 6x6 board of scattered letter blocks. Slide the blocks one square at a time to spell the category's words across or down, then clear them; clear every block to win. Words cross and share blocks, so the order you clear them in matters. A short adventure ties it together: Shingo, a Japanese boy on a homestay in America, sets off with the archaeologist Professor McManan's spoiled daughter Milly and his assistant Ian to search seven ruins for crystal plates and rescue the missing professor. The title is a pun: 娯楽王 "king of fun" written with 語 "word".

Sanzo's party has lost the Three Aspects' credit card and ran up a bill eating and fighting at an inn. To pay it off, they run festival food stalls for the four sisters who own the inn: Meifan, Loran, Liyi and Xiao. You pick a sister, roll dice on a town board, place signs that bring customers to the stalls, meet lucky and unlucky events and play Blackjack, until the debt is paid.

**Harobots** (ハロボッツ) is Sunrise Interactive's 1999 robot-raising RPG for the original (monochrome) WonderSwan, released only in Japan. It retells the first Dragon Ball saga, from Goku meeting Bulma to King Piccolo, as a board game: you move along the map with cards, meet the characters of the series, and fight with a card system where stars, move types and numbers decide who hits. Master Roshi, Korin and Mr. Popo train you in the rules.

produced_by.notes:
**Riviera - Yakusoku no Chi Riviera** is Sting's 2002 RPG for the WonderSwan Color, published by Bandai and released only in Japan. Most people know it from the later Game Boy Advance and PSP remakes, but it started on the WonderSwan Color. A thousand years after Ragnarok, the war between the gods of Asgard and the demons of Utgard, the Seven Magi send two Grim Angels, Ein and Ledah, to the island of Riviera to unleash Retribution, the hidden power of the gods, because the demons seem to be coming back. Ein loses his memory, wakes up in Elendia, a village of sprites, and goes on with Rose, his familiar, and the girls he meets there: Fia, Lina, Serene and Cierra.

This patch translates the WonderSwan Color original into English.

**Ring Infinity** is a horror sound novel released only in Japan by Kadokawa Shoten and Bandai for the WonderSwan in August 2000. It is set in the world of Koji Suzuki's *Ring*: a rumour about a cursed video that kills whoever watches it exactly one week later, students dying of heart failure, e-mail pals, a "cursed homepage" and the shadow of Sadako Yamamura. You read the story and pick what to say and do; your choices open different branches and endings over three chapters.

This patch translates it into English.

**What is translated**

- The whole story (about 4,300 screens of text), the choices, the menus, the save/delete dialogs and the staff roll labels.
- The Japanese original shows the text vertically; the English is shown in horizontal lines with a new variable-width font, in the same window under the pictures.
- Text drawn as pictures: the WonderGate dialogs ("Connect?", "Connection failed."...) and the Japanese inside some scene pictures (the "Suicide Diary" web page, the mail program, a scream).
- **WonderGate unlock:** the Mobile WonderGate service is long gone, but its content is in the game. produced_by.notes:
**Riviera - Yakusoku no Chi Riviera** is Sting's 2002 RPG for the WonderSwan Color, published by Bandai and released only in Japan. Most people know it from the later Game Boy Advance and PSP remakes, but it started on the WonderSwan Color. A thousand years after Ragnarok, the war between the gods of Asgard and the demons of Utgard, the Seven Magi send two Grim Angels, Ein and Ledah, to the island of Riviera to unleash Retribution, the hidden power of the gods, because the demons seem to be coming back. Ein loses his memory, wakes up in Elendia, a village of sprites, and goes on with Rose, his familiar, and the girls he meets there: Fia, Lina, Serene and Cierra.

This patch translates the WonderSwan Color original into English.

**Digital Monster: D-Project** is a 2002 Bandai Digimon raising and adventure game for the WonderSwan Color that never left Japan. The game you just bought has been "hacked": its data is being erased, and Ophanimon pulls you inside to repair it. You hatch Digimon with the Egg Machine, raise them, walk the broken areas of the Digital World, fight with up to three partners, and restore the lost land by bringing new Digimon to life. It also links with the Pendulum and D-Power toys of the time.

This patch translates it into English.

> **Please read:** this translation was made **entirely with AI** (Claude), as a personal project. I'm sharing it as it is for anyone who wants to play, but it must **never be uploaded to romhacking sites** (romhacking.net and the like): it isn't up to the standard of a real fan translation and it doesn't belong there.

**Reference guide**

Terms, area names and menu names follow **"WSC Digimon D-project ENG Guide" by DigiKidult**, an English guide translated from his Chinese one: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1FWjNVGwpuqjQgj14EFWB6HkTaJqRKSe6x0xbiW-z2aw/htmlview

Many thanks to DigiKidult. Keep the guide open while you play: it has the egg codes, item codes, Digivolution requirements and the story route.

**What's translated**

* The whole script: the "hacked" opening and the data erasure, Ophanimon, every story event, the Sovereigns, the villains and the ending.
* Menus: field menu (Items, Digimon, Call Back, Map, Save), items and …

**Why a new translation?**
The WonderSwan Color Final Fantasy was never released outside Japan. The only English patch for it so far is Kalas’s v0.91 from 2002, which was never finished. The game has had several official English releases since, but all of them are other remakes (PS1 Origins, GBA Dawn of Souls, PSP, Pixel Remaster), and each one adapted the script and renamed things in its own way. The NES version itself has a different set of names again. Copying any of those scripts would have meant choosing one of these adaptations and stitching it onto text it was never written for.

So this translation starts again from the Japanese text of the WonderSwan Color ROM, and the whole game is translated: dialogue, menus, battle text, the opening narration and the graphics. Names follow the official Japanese names of this version, written in English, with no Western renames. Some will look unfamiliar if you grew up with the NES version (Lukahn, Onlak, the Lufeinians...).
This is intentional: they are what the Japanese text says, chosen by comparing several glossaries and a human vote.

The Palamecian Empire has summoned monsters from the Underworld to conquer the world, and Firion, Maria and Guy, who lost their parents when the Empire attacked Fynn, join Princess Hilda's rebels.

The WonderSwan Color Final Fantasy II was never released outside Japan. The only English patch for it so far, RPGOne’s “Stage 1” v0.97 from 2002, was never finished. Its script was adapted from Neo Demiforce’s translation of the NES version rather than translated from this one, the intro was left in Japanese, and its own readme lists the battle menus and the shop Yes/No as not displaying correctly. The planned full “Stage 2” never came out. The official English releases (Origins, Dawn of Souls, PSP, Pixel Remaster) are other remakes, and each adapts the script and the names differently: the same town is Altair, the same spell is Life or something else, depending on which version you played.

**Why a new translation?**
The WonderSwan Color Final Fantasy was never released outside Japan. The only English patch for it so far is Kalas’s v0.91 from 2002, which was never finished. The game has had several official English releases since, but all of them are other remakes (PS1 Origins, GBA Dawn of Souls, PSP, Pixel Remaster), and each one adapted the script and renamed things in its own way. The NES version itself has a different set of names again. Copying any of those scripts would have meant choosing one of these adaptations and stitching it onto text it was never written for.

So this translation starts again from the Japanese text of the WonderSwan Color ROM, and the whole game is translated: dialogue, menus, battle text, the opening narration and the graphics. Names follow the official Japanese names of this version, written in English, with no Western renames. Some will look unfamiliar if you grew up with the NES version (Lukahn, Onlak, the Lufeinians...).
This is intentional: they are what the Japanese text says, chosen by comparing several glossaries and a human vote.

**Final Fantasy II** for the WonderSwan Color is Square's 2001 remake of the second Final Fantasy, released only in Japan. The Palamecian Empire has summoned monsters from the Underworld to conquer the world, and Firion, Maria and Guy, who lost their parents when the Empire attacked Fynn, join Princess Hilda's rebels.

**Why a new translation?**
The WonderSwan Color Final Fantasy II was never released outside Japan. The only English patch for it so far, RPGOne’s “Stage 1” v0.97 from 2002, was never finished. Its script was adapted from Neo Demiforce’s translation of the NES version rather than translated from this one, the intro was left in Japanese, and its own readme lists the battle menus and the shop Yes/No as not displaying correctly. The planned full “Stage 2” never came out. The official English releases (Origins, Dawn of Souls, PSP, Pixel Remaster) are other remakes, and each adapts the script and the names differently: the same town is Altair, the same spell is Life or something else, depending on which version you played.

So this translation starts again from the Japanese text of the WonderSwan Color ROM, and the whole game is in English: dialogue, keywords, menus, battle text, the demo captions and the graphics. For names, the rule is simple.
Square Enix’s official English is kept wherever it matches the Japanese (Firion, Maria, Guy, Minwu, Hilda, Palamecia, Wild Rose, Mythril...). Where every English release changed the name, the form faithful to the Japanese is …

**Note:** a complete human translation by filler & Supper already exists, and it's the recommended one if it works for you. This patch is an independent alternative. It also keeps the ROM at 512 KB, so it runs on **GGSWAN** on the WonderSwan.

**What's translated**
- Main menu, speech bubble and mini-game menu
- All mini-game instructions and bonus-game messages
- Quiz World: every question and answer
- Ending lines
- Title banners, Rei's fortune screens and the password screen label

Text is ALL CAPS. Names follow the current official English dub (Viz): Usagi, Chibiusa, Rei, Ami, Makoto, Minako, Haruka, Michiru, Tuxedo Mask, Death Busters, Holy Grail, Sailor Guardians.

**How it was made**
1. Claude analysed the ROM with a small Game Gear emulator it wrote in Python. It found the text engine, the tile compression (an RLE split into two byte streams) and the quiz pointer tables.
2. Claude translated the full script from the Japanese.
3. ChatGPT did a full semantic review of every line against the Japanese, in blocks.
4. Claude checked and applied the corrections and rebuilt the ROM.

**Ring Infinity** is a horror sound novel released only in Japan by Kadokawa Shoten and Bandai for the WonderSwan in August 2000. It is set in the world of Koji Suzuki's *Ring*: a rumour about a cursed video that kills whoever watches it exactly one week later, students dying of heart failure, e-mail pals, a "cursed homepage" and the shadow of Sadako Yamamura. You read the story and pick what to say and do; your choices open different branches and endings over three chapters.

This patch translates it into English.

**What is translated**

- The whole story (about 4,300 screens of text), the choices, the menus, the save/delete dialogs and the staff roll labels.
- The Japanese original shows the text vertically; the English is shown in horizontal lines with a new variable-width font, in the same window under the pictures.
- Text drawn as pictures: the WonderGate dialogs ("Connect?", "Connection failed."...) and the Japanese inside some scene pictures (the "Suicide Diary" web page, the mail program, a scream).
- **WonderGate unlock:** the Mobile WonderGate service is long gone, but its content is in the game. The patch unlocks it: "Bonus scenarios" (an extra scenario, a different take on the first chapter) and "Read mail" (31 mails from other players, shown one after another each time you open it) appear in the title menu.

**SD Gundam G Generation: Gather Beat 2** (SDガンダム Gジェネレーション ギャザービート2) is Bandai's 2001 G Generation strategy game for the WonderSwan Color, released only in Japan. You command a mixed force of mobile suits and ships from across the Gundam series on grid maps, replaying battles from Mobile Suit Gundam, The 08th MS Team, 0083, Zeta, ZZ, Char's Counterattack, Victory, G Gundam, Gundam Wing, Gundam X, Turn A and more. Pilots fire ID commands (special abilities with their own speech), between stages you manage the Backstage (buying, developing and modifying units, assigning pilots), and the game adds an encyclopedia of characters and mobile suits, adventure scenes, two endings and unit trading over the link cable. This patch translates it into English. (The first Gather Beat has its own patch and release.)

> **Please read:** this translation was made **with AI** (Claude), as a hobby project. A person (me) made every judgement call before release, but nobody on the project is a professional translator. I'm sharing it as it is for anyone who wants to play. Please **don't upload it to romhacking sites** (romhacking.net and the like). It may not be up to the standard of a real fan translation and it doesn't belong there.

**What's translated**

* All story, map and battle dialogue, ID and battle speech, the adventure scenes, menus and names, the encyclopedia (684 entries), and the narration of both endings.
